tagline.text: Three turquoise falls and cliff-diving pools in the forest

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,250–4,050 (Manila day round trip, by bus or private car)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), about 6 hours by road

children.text: Bolinao Falls is a set of three waterfalls in the forest of Bolinao, on the western edge of Pangasinan. Each has a deep swimming pool and cliff-diving spots, and the entrance fees are low, so it makes an easy stop alongside Patar Beach and the caves.

Bolinao Falls sits in Barangay Samang Norte on the Bolinao peninsula, at the far northwestern tip of Pangasinan. It is not one big waterfall but a name for three falls strung along the same stream. Locals call them Falls 1, Falls 2 and Falls 3, and each has its own entrance and ticket booth. Because the water runs through limestone country, the swimming pools glow in pale emerald and turquoise.

Bolinao is better known for Patar White Beach, its caves and the Cape Bolinao Lighthouse, so the falls tend to be quieter. They lie a bit farther west of Alaminos, the gateway to the Hundred Islands, so most visitors focus on the beaches and squeeze in one or two falls along the way. On a weekday morning you can sometimes have a whole pool almost to yourself.

The appeal for travelers is simple. In the midday heat of northern Luzon you can cool off in fresh water instead of the sea. Falls 1 has a cliff-jumping spot two storeys high that is popular with kids and younger travelers. Falls 2 has a wide pool with varied depths that suits families, and cottages are available to rent. Falls 3 gets the fewest visitors and is the pick if you want a calm dip.

The bus from Manila takes about 6 hours, so a day trip is tight. We recommend staying at least one night in Bolinao town or near Patar Beach and combining the beach, caves and falls. This guide compares several travel blogs and local information, and fees change from year to year, so check with the Bolinao tourism office or recent visitor reports before you go. A little local context helps too. The falls are small attractions run by villagers, and the ticket staff often guide visitors and keep the site clean. The fees are small but go directly to the community, so pay the posted price instead of haggling, and renting a cottage or buying snacks helps even more. Weekends and public holidays bring large family groups from Pangasinan and Manila and can get noisy, so choose a weekday if you want quiet.

This has the highest cliff of the three falls, with a diving spot two storeys above the water. The pool is deep enough that people reportedly jump both with and without a life vest. The walk in from the road is short, about 5–10 minutes.

blocks.title: The wide swimming pool at Falls 2

children.text: The deepest part of the pool is described as about 18 feet (about 5.5 m). The edges have shallow areas that are easy to manage with children, and cottages for rent make it a good place to unpack a packed lunch and rest. It is about a 10-minute walk from Falls 1, or a short tricycle ride.

It combines features of Falls 1 and 2, with a large area for swimming and rafting and a small jumping zone. Few people come and the surroundings are less developed, so it keeps a natural feel. Mobile signal is weak, so download directions in advance.

The Bolinao area is coral limestone, and minerals in the water tint the pools a pale turquoise. The color is sharpest on a clear morning when the sun hits the water, and after several days of rain the water turns cloudy, so pick your day by the weather.

The three falls are close together, so you can hire one tricycle to take you around in one go. Each has its own entrance fee, so visiting all of them adds up a little. If you only want one, active travelers should choose Falls 1 and families should choose Falls 2.

blocks.title: Pairing with Patar Beach and the caves

children.text: The falls are on the same peninsula as Patar White Beach, the Cape Bolinao Lighthouse and Enchanted Cave. The most natural plan is the falls in the morning, then the beach and a sunset spot in the afternoon.
Entrance is around ₱50 per fall and parking is a small fee. Unlike famous falls elsewhere, you do not need an expensive guided package, so it is easy to drop in.
Have breakfast in Bolinao town or Patar and find a tricycle. Tell the driver you want to visit all three falls and agree on the fare first.
If you have not yet paid the
environmental and registration fee
, pay it at the information booth. Keep the receipt, since it covers other attractions for several days.
Arrive at Falls 1, pay the entrance fee and walk 5–10 minutes along the forest trail. Dive and swim while it is still quiet.
Move on to Falls 2. Rent a cottage to leave your things and relax in the wide pool.
Have lunch nearby or eat the packed lunch you brought. The stalls around the falls mostly sell snacks.
Visit Falls 3, then head back to town or to Patar Beach.
Mornings are quieter and the water color is better. After lunch, more local family groups arrive.
Take an early bus from Manila to Bolinao and leave your bags at your lodging.
Visit Falls 1 and Falls 2, then watch the sunset at Patar Beach and the Cape Bolinao Lighthouse later in the afternoon.
Explore caves such as Enchanted Cave, or go out to Alaminos for a Hundred Islands boat tour.
See St. James the Great Church in town, buy some binungey, a local snack, and board the bus back to Manila.

Bus companies such as Five Star, Victory Liner and Dagupan Bus run direct trips to Bolinao from the Cubao and Pasay terminals in Manila. The one-way fare is reported at around ₱450–500 (2024; the air-con bus is listed at ₱459) and the trip at about 6 hours.
You can also take a bus to Alaminos and then continue about 1 hour by bus or van to Bolinao.
Schedules and fares change often, so check the company's latest announcements before you travel.
A same-day round trip from Manila is tiring. We recommend staying one night in Bolinao.
From Manila, connect SCTEX, TPLEX and the expressway toward Alaminos for about 5–6 hours. One blog estimated round-trip fuel at about ₱2,000–2,500 and tolls at ₱500–700 each way.
Parking at the falls is reported at about ₱20 for motorcycles and about ₱30 for cars.
Victory Liner runs from Baguio (Gov. Pack Road) to Bolinao, reportedly from ₱237 one way and about 8 hours.
A tricycle is the easiest way from Bolinao town to the falls. Enter Bolinao Falls 1 in your map app to find the location.
One blog lists a tricycle from town to the falls at ₱150–200, and a jeepney from Alaminos at ₱50–100. Always agree on the fare before boarding.
A 2017 record puts a tricycle tour of the whole peninsula at about ₱1,500 for four people, but prices are likely higher now.

For both swimming and getting around, the November–May dry season is best. The water is clear and the paths are dry, so you are less likely to slip. In March–May the sun is strong and the cool falls are especially welcome.

In the June–October rainy season the flow increases, and the pools can turn cloudy and the paths slippery. On days with a typhoon warning, both the sea and streams are dangerous, so postpone your trip.

items.label: Falls entrance
items.note: Reported as around ₱50 for Falls 1 and 2 and ₱20 for Falls 3 (2024–2025 sources; some list a single ₱20 fee, so confirm locally)

items.label: Environmental and registration fee
items.note: Common to all Bolinao attractions (₱25 environmental + ₱15 registration), valid 4 days. An October 2025 report also confirms an ID check and a ₱40 fee per person

items.label: Life vest rental
items.note: Recommended if you are not a confident swimmer

items.label: Bus from Manila
items.note: From Cubao and Pasay, about 6 hours (2024 source: ₱450–500)

There is almost no lodging around the falls. Guesthouses and small resorts cluster in Bolinao town and around Patar White Beach, and cheaper ones start from around ₱500. Some places at Patar also let you pitch a tent. Book early for the April–May peak season and long weekends.

At the falls, expect only simple snacks from the stalls, and either have lunch at a restaurant in town or bring a packed lunch. Local specialties include binungey, a sticky rice cake, and maratangtang, a sea urchin dish sold at Patar Beach. Seafood prices depend on the market, so ask before you order.
Bring light clothes to wear over your swimsuit, water shoes and a towel. The rocks are slippery.
If you are not a strong swimmer, rent a life vest. At the diving spots, check the depth and the rocks below with your own eyes first.
Carry plenty of cash. Cards are not accepted at the falls, and ATMs are far away in town.
Arriving early helps you avoid crowds and gets you better water color.
Camping is reportedly not allowed at the falls, so stay in town or at Patar.
For a drone, get permission from the local staff or a guide.
Take all your trash with you. Carrying out food wrappers and single-use plastic is basic etiquette.
Mobile signal is weak in places, so download an offline map.
On weekends, arrive around 8:00 AM to get a cottage. On weekdays you can usually rent one on the spot.
Avoid entering the water or diving when the flow is high after rain or the water is cloudy. Cliff diving is at your own risk.
The depth at diving spots changes with the season and water level, so check before you jump.
Rocky paths and pool edges are slippery. Water shoes are safer than sandals.
Always keep a close eye on children and put a life vest on them.
Fees and opening hours differ between sources and may have changed. Check the latest announcement.
Leave valuables in the cottage or the car and carry only the minimum.
The town at the center of the area, good for combining with the church, beaches and caves.
A white-sand beach a short tricycle ride from the falls, with sunsets and beachside lodging.
An American-era lighthouse near Patar Beach, free to enter and beautiful at dusk.
